d: A written agreement, signed by the future spouses before the marriage, that fixes their property relations during the marriage.
x: It must be executed before the wedding. It binds third persons only when registered.

d: A donation made before the celebration of the marriage, in consideration of the marriage, in favor of one or both of the future spouses.
x: A gift between spouses after the wedding is not a donation propter nuptias; it is generally void.

d: The property regime in which all property owned by the spouses at the time of the marriage or acquired after it becomes common property, except what the law excludes.
x: It is the default regime for marriages after August 3, 1988, when there is no valid marriage settlement.

d: The property regime in which each spouse keeps his or her own property, while the fruits of that property and what they earn or acquire by effort or chance go to a common fund, whose net gains are divided equally when it ends.
x: Unlike ACP, property brought into the marriage and property bought with exclusive money stay exclusive.

d: The property regime in which each spouse owns, administers, enjoys and disposes of his or her own property, without the other's consent.
x: Family expenses are still shared, in proportion to income, and the spouses are solidarily liable to creditors for them.

d: Property of a spouse that does not form part of the community or the partnership, and so belongs to that spouse alone.
x: What counts as exclusive differs between ACP and CPG.

d: Leaving the conjugal dwelling without intention of returning. Being gone for three months, or failing to give news of one's whereabouts within that time, is prima facie proof of it.
x: A spouse who simply moved out for a while but keeps in touch and supports the family has not abandoned the family.

d: Spouses living apart without a court decree. It does not dissolve their property regime.
x: It becomes a ground for judicial separation of property only after at least one year, with reconciliation highly improbable.

d: The process, after the regime ends, of listing the property, paying the debts, returning each spouse's exclusive property, and dividing what is left.
x: The first step is always an inventory that lists the common property and each spouse's exclusive property separately.

d: The value of the legitime of the common children, computed at the time of liquidation and delivered to them when the property regime is liquidated.
x: It is delivered during the parents' lifetime, in cash, property or sound securities.

d: The family's home, which at liquidation goes to the spouse with whom the majority of the common children choose to remain.
x: Children below 7 are deemed to choose the mother, unless the court decides otherwise.

d: A personal debt or liability of one spouse that the community or partnership pays when that spouse has no exclusive property, and that is deducted from his or her share at liquidation.
x: It is not a gift. The paying regime is repaid from the spouse's share.

d: A court order, during the marriage, that ends the spouses' community or partnership and gives each spouse his or her own property from then on.
x: During the marriage, the regime can change only by court order. A private agreement is not enough.

d: The restoration, by court order, of the property regime the spouses had before a judicial separation of property, when the cause of the separation has ended.
x: After a voluntary separation is revived, no new voluntary separation may be granted.

d: The co-ownership between a man and a woman who are free to marry each other and live together as husband and wife without a valid marriage. Their wages and the property they acquire together are owned in equal shares.
x: Care of the home counts as a contribution here, but not under Art. 148.

d: The co-ownership in all other cohabitation, where only property acquired by the actual joint contribution of money, property or industry is owned in common, in proportion to the contributions.
x: There is no presumption of joint effort. Contribution must be proved.

d: The relations between husband and wife, parents and children, other ascendants and descendants, and brothers and sisters, whether of the full or half blood.
x: The list is exclusive. In-laws, uncles, nephews and cousins are not included.

d: Genuine attempts to settle a dispute between family members, which a verified complaint must show were made and failed before a suit between them can prosper.
x: A successful compromise is not required, only the attempt and its failure.

d: The dwelling house where the family lives and the land on which it stands. It is constituted from the time it is occupied as the family residence.
x: No registration is needed under the Family Code, and a person may have only one family home.

d: The spouses or an unmarried head of family, and their parents, ascendants, descendants, brothers and sisters who live in the family home and depend on the head of the family for legal support.
x: Living in the house is not enough. The person must depend on the head of the family for support.

d: A child conceived or born during a valid marriage.
x: The mother's declaration against legitimacy, or even her conviction for adultery, does not change the status.

d: A child conceived and born outside a valid marriage.
x: Both conception and birth must be outside marriage. One inside makes the child legitimate.

d: The legal relationship between a parent and a child, which may be by nature (legitimate or illegitimate) or by adoption.
x: Filiation is proved by primary evidence first, and by secondary evidence only when primary evidence is absent.

d: A direct action by the husband, or by his heirs in limited cases, to prove that a child born during the marriage is not his.
x: Legitimacy cannot be attacked collaterally, and the mother or another man cannot bring this action.

t: Open and continuous possession of the status of a child
d: The parent's consistent and continuous treatment of a person as his or her child, shown by acts of the parent and the family.
x: It is secondary evidence. For an illegitimate child, an action based on it must be brought during the alleged parent's lifetime.

d: The process by which a child conceived and born outside marriage becomes legitimate through the later valid marriage of the parents.
x: At conception, the parents must have had no impediment to marry each other, except minority.

d: The legal process that gives a child a permanent family by making the adoptee the legitimate child of the adopter.
x: It severs legal ties with the biological parents, except a biological parent who is the adopter's spouse.

t: Certificate Declaring a Child Legally Available for Adoption (CDCLAA)
d: The document that declares a child free for adoption, needed before a child who is not a relative or stepchild can be placed for adoption.
x: Under current law it is issued by the National Authority for Child Care.

d: The undoing of an adoption at the request of the adoptee, on serious grounds such as repeated maltreatment, an attempt on the adoptee's life, sexual assault or violence, or abandonment.
x: Only the adoptee may ask for it. The adopter's remedy is disinheritance.

d: Everything indispensable for sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical attendance, education and transportation, in keeping with the family's financial capacity.
x: Education is included even beyond the age of majority.

d: Support that was already due but was not paid.
src: Civil Code, Art. 301; Family Code, Art. 203
x: Unlike future support, it may be renounced, compromised or set off.

d: Support given under an agreement or a will, rather than by force of law.
x: The amount beyond legal support may be attached or executed upon.

d: The rights and duties of parents over the person and property of their unemancipated children, for the children's upbringing and welfare.
x: It cannot be renounced or transferred, except as the law allows, as in adoption.

d: The parental authority exercised, when the parents are dead, absent or unsuitable, by the surviving grandparent, then the oldest sibling over 21, then the child's actual custodian over 21.
x: Those exercising it are only subsidiarily liable for the child's acts.

d: The authority and responsibility of schools, their administrators and teachers, and child-care institutions over minors under their supervision, instruction or custody.
x: They are principally and solidarily liable for the minor's acts; the parents are only subsidiarily liable.

d: The rule that no child under 7 shall be separated from the mother, unless the court finds compelling reasons.
x: Compelling reasons include neglect, abandonment, drug addiction and similar unfitness, not merely the father's greater wealth.

d: The end of parental authority over a child's person and property, which happens when the child reaches 18.
x: Parental consent is still needed to marry until 21.

d: A person who has disappeared from his domicile and whose whereabouts are unknown, and who may be judicially declared absent after 2 years without news, or 5 years if he left an administrator.
x: A declaration of absence is about managing his property. It does not presume him dead.

d: The legal presumption that an absent person is dead after the period set by law: 7 years in general, or 4 years when he disappeared in danger of death.
src: Civil Code, Arts. 390–391; Family Code, Art. 41
x: To remarry, the present spouse needs 4 years (2 in danger cases), a well-founded belief, and a court declaration.

d: A harmless, obvious mistake in writing, copying or typing an entry in the civil register that can be corrected by reference to other records.
x: It may be corrected by the civil registrar. Substantial changes, such as legitimacy or citizenship, need a court.
